ruling.reasoning:
The trip was RydeTAXI, so the fare is metered and extra kilometres reach the rider's bill [F7]. The trace settles that exactly one off-route segment exists [F3] and that the RD-4 incident screen fails — no qualifying incident, and a speed band alone does not exempt [F15]. So the segment stands or falls on RD-5 consent, which the trace leaves to me.

On consent: the rider's own message at 17:21 is "随便你，哪条快走哪条，我赶时间" [F9], sent before the segment began at 17:24 [F3], and it is a general delegation of route choice — both advocates read it that way and I read it the same, so at the level of kind of agreement there is nothing to send back. The driver's pre-segment message named only the road to be avoided, not a route to be taken [F8], so this is not named-road consent and G13 does not arise; a driver-statement claim of consent would not count under G11, but here the consent is in the rider's own message, so the statement [F11] adds nothing [F9][F8][RD-5].

The question is scope. RD-5's general-route branch covers "a route chosen to get there", and excludes an errand of the driver's own — a stop away from the route or a loop that reaches nothing [F9][F3]. The driver admits there was no stop and the record shows none: the single segment runs continuously from 17:24 to 17:40 to the destination corridor, without any stop or destination-less loop [F3]. The rider's counter-argument is that the loop was too long (10.28 km driven where 2.75 km sufficed, +7.53 km, up to 2273 m lateral) and was not in fact faster [F3][F2]. But length and inefficacy are not the RD-5 exclusions — the policy puts no kilometre or metre ceiling on a general route authorisation, and "a route chosen to get there" that turns out slower is still a route chosen to get there, not an errand. The congestion the driver flagged was on the road the rider himself acknowledged ("哪条快走哪条" answers a question about a jam) and the flagged expressway was genuinely at band 2 (10–19 km/h) at the moment of the decision [F12]. Reading the rider's words in context, the agreement covers the segment driven. On the stipulated general_route_consent ground the consequence is exempt [F8][F9][F12][RD-5].

With the only segment exempt, there are no unexempted kilometres. The trace's allowed outcomes are refund_partial, no_action or escalate; the formula Σ extra_km × $1.4099/km yields Σ = 0 km × $1.4099/km = $0.00, and a refund of 0 is no_action under RD-2. The rider's figure of $10.62 (7.53 km × $1.4099/km, derived from the trip rate $43.20 ÷ 30.64 km = $1.4099/km) is arithmetically sound but rests on the segment being unexempted [F3][F4][F7], which it is not.

Account action: RD-6 requires route_disputes_upheld_90d ≥ 1 for the driver; the trace records 0 [F18], and profile facts cannot decide the case anyway. No flag_account.

The complaint is a fare complaint; the chats are a jam-avoidance exchange and a route delegation; the statement is a route explanation. Nothing reads as a threat, intimidation, harassment, sexual remark or dangerous-driving allegation. Finding: none [SAFE-1][SAFE-2].

Evidence: the chat record is complete and every message is timestamped [F10], the segment is measured [F3], the fare breakdown is on the record [F7] and the traffic screen is closed [F15]. Nothing my ruling needs is missing.
